text:
Sampled HR@10 and full-catalog ranking measure different tasks. Krichene–Rendle show sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation; a sequential-recommendation study finds inconsistencies with both uniform and popularity sampling. Thus, large training margins against sampled negatives cannot establish strong full-catalog ranking. A 2025 study further distinguishes candidate-sampling bias from exposure bias: even full-catalog evaluation against logged interactions does not reveal all true preferences. [Sampled metrics](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/), [sequential evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.13045), [2025 reliability study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05398).

Suggested diagnostics, inferred from these findings: measure positive-item rank, fraction of eligible negatives outranking it, and pairwise win rate alongside sampled training margins. These rank-based quantities avoid dependence on score scale; retain explicit tie handling. Stratify validation hits by target popularity and user history length, using training interactions to define bins. For the twenty training users’ full-catalog recommendations, report catalog coverage, popularity distribution and concentration; these describe recommendation behavior, not relevance or causal exposure bias. Distribution-aware evaluation research supports examining subgroup outcomes rather than averages alone. [Distributionally-Informed Evaluation, 2024](https://841.io/doc/disteval.html).

Keep all four categories and the pinned macro validation HR@10 unchanged. For uncertainty, use a paired user bootstrap within each category: resample the same user indices across compared models, recompute category HR@10, then average the four category scores equally. Report a 95% interval for the improvement. This proposed procedure quantifies user-sampling uncertainty conditional on the fixed candidates and trained models; it does not capture training-seed variation, candidate-sampling uncertainty or repeated-search selection bias.
